sections.title: Daily Market Report
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* The Daily Market Report is the market-wide backdrop, the same whichever symbol you are looking at. It shows what the app's macro pass stored on its latest run (it runs every six hours): four macro stances built from public economic data, a reading of how they fit together, a market-cycle reading built on SPY, prices and price phases for a fixed list of instruments and your Watchlist, calendar context, and market-wide headlines. Every label is a fixed rule applied to stored numbers; the report describes the backdrop and does not predict what markets will do.

entries.title: Report time and the top strip

blocks.text: Under the page title, **Report generated** gives the time of the newest reading the macro pass stored, in your local time, followed by that day's date. The pass runs every six hours and the page loads the latest report once, without refreshing. If the newest reading is more than 12 hours old, a note above it reads "This report is more than 12 hours old — showing the most recent available.": the pass has stopped updating, and the page shows the last report rather than nothing. Before any report exists it reads "No report has been generated yet."

The strip at the top of **Market overview** shows three market numbers, each with the date of the observation it shows, not the report's date. All three come from FRED, the St. Louis Fed's public data service, which publishes them with a delay, so they are often several days behind the market. A number with no observation in the last 60 days shows "—" and "no recent observation".

items: **VIX** — the CBOE Volatility Index's daily close: the S&P 500 volatility the options market expects over the next 30 days. Beside it sits the app's band for that same observation, with its icon: **normal** from 12 to 20 (circled tick), **elevated** above 20 up to 35 (circled dash), **extreme fear** above 35 (warning triangle) and **complacency** below 12 (also a warning triangle: very low volatility is read as calm but vulnerable, not as good news). The band appears only when it was worked out for the very observation shown; otherwise the number stands alone.
**10Y yield** — the 10-year US Treasury yield, in percent. No band and no icon.
**EUR/USD** — US dollars per euro. No band and no icon.

blocks.text: The first four cards — **Monetary Policy**, **Growth Cycle**, **Inflation** and **Global/Geopolitical Stress** — each sum up one area of the economy from public FRED data. Each shows a **stance** word with its icon, a **Score** and an as-of date. **Signals (N)** opens the rows the stance was built from, grouped under headings such as "Tier 1 · Leading Indicators": tier 1 is the app's primary read for that area, and the grouping is for reading only — each row's weight is set separately, as each card's entry below lists.

Each row shows its name, its latest value, its label and an as-of date. Values are shown without units (the Treasury yields excepted); each card's entry gives them. Stance words and labels are the stored codes with the underscores shown as spaces — for example tight labor — and are not otherwise reworded. A stance with no data at all reads insufficient data with the no-data icon; a card whose stance was never stored shows "no data".

The **Score** is a weighted average of the card's scored rows. Each row's label carries a fixed score and each row a fixed weight; rows with no data are left out rather than counted as zero, and the result always lies between −1 and +1. Fixed cut-offs turn it into the stance word. **The direction differs by card**: on Monetary Policy and Growth Cycle a higher score is the easier backdrop (accommodative, expansion), while on Inflation and Global/Geopolitical Stress a higher score means more inflation pressure or more stress. Some rows are shown for context only and do not count; the card entries say which.

The icon beside a stance or a row comes from the tone the app stored with its label when it computed it, never from the page: a circled tick for **constructive**, a circled dash for **neutral**, a warning triangle for **stressed**, a dashed circle for **no data**. The Treasury yields row, which shows levels rather than a classification, has no icon. The tone is a fixed reading of each label, looked up in a table kept per row, so the same word can carry different icons on different rows. A row's icon reads that row on its own terms, not the way it moves the card's score: on the Inflation card, a copper price up 10% or more on the year reads global expansion with a tick, while adding to the inflation score. These icons, in the Market overview card, are the only status colours on the page.

The **as of** date on a stance and on each row is the day the app last worked the reading out — it does so on every six-hourly run — not the date of the data behind it. Monthly and quarterly figures keep the value of their latest release between releases, so a row can read "as of" today while its figure is weeks or months old. A row whose source series has stopped updating altogether — its newest observation older than a limit set for how often that series is published — reads **no recent data** with the no-data icon, shows no value and is left out of the card's score; the LEI and China GDP rows read this way today.

How loose or tight financial conditions are, from the Federal Reserve's policy rate to credit markets. Stance: **accommodative** above 0.40 (tick), **neutral** above −0.40 up to 0.40 (dash), **restrictive** at −0.40 or below (warning triangle); a score of exactly 0.40 reads neutral. Weights: Rate, Yield curve and Credit spread 2 each, Real rate 1.5, Balance sheet and Breakeven inflation 1 each, M2 supply 0.5.

items: **Balance sheet** — the Federal Reserve's total assets, in billions of dollars (6,747.7 is about $6.7 trillion): **qe** when they grew by more than $100 billion over the last four weeks, **qt** when they shrank by more than $100 billion, otherwise **neutral**.

**Credit spread** — the extra yield on US high-yield ("junk") corporate bonds over Treasuries, in basis points (280 is 2.80 percentage points): **benign** up to 300, **elevated** above 300, **crisis** above 600.

**Rate** — the effective federal funds rate, in percent. The label compares it with twelve months earlier: **hiking** after a rise of more than 0.25 points, **cutting** after a fall of more than 0.25 points, otherwise **neutral**.
**Real rate** — the 10-year inflation-protected Treasury (TIPS) yield, in percent: **deeply negative** below −2, **balanced** from −2 up to 2, **headwind** at 2 or above.

**Yield curve** — the 10-year Treasury yield minus the 2-year, in percentage points: **steep** above 1.0, **normal** above 0 up to 1.0, **flat** above −0.5 up to 0, **inverted** at −0.5 or below. It reads **re steepening** instead when, within the last 90 daily readings, the curve fell below −0.5 and it is now above 0 and more than 0.5 points above that low.

**Breakeven inflation** — the yearly inflation rate the bond market is pricing in over ten years, in percent: **anchored** up to 2.5, **rising** above 2.5, **unanchored** above 3.0. Rising is a level, not a trend.
**M2 supply** — growth of the M2 money supply over twelve months, in percent: **inflationary** above 15, **normal** from 4 to 15, **slow** from 0 to 4, **deflationary** below 0.
**Treasury yields** — the 2-, 10- and 30-year Treasury yields as plain levels, with no label and no icon. They do not count toward the score.

blocks.text: Whether the US economy is expanding or slowing, from jobs, output, spending and business data. Stance: **expansion** at 0.40 or above (tick), **slowdown** in between (dash), **contraction** at −0.40 or below (warning triangle). Weights: PMI 0.15, GDP and Employment 0.14 each, LEI 0.12 (not counted today, see below), Consumer 0.10, Claims and Housing 0.08 each, Capex and Consumer sentiment 0.05 each, averaged over the rows that have data. **PMI**, the ISM manufacturing survey, always reads no data: its FRED series is not available to the app, so it never counts.

items: **LEI** — reads **no recent data** and does not count. The app's leading-index series is FRED's Leading Index for the United States (the Philadelphia Fed's), which was discontinued: its last observation is February 2020. A reading whose newest observation is more than 120 days old (a monthly series, normally one to two months behind) is treated as no recent data: it shows no value and is left out of the Growth score. The Conference Board's Leading Economic Index is not available to the app, and no other series is substituted for it.
**Claims** — initial jobless claims, averaged over the last four weeks: **tight labor** below 225,000, **normal** below 300,000, **normalizing** below 500,000, **crisis** from 500,000.
**Housing** — housing starts, in thousands of homes a year at the current pace: **strong** from 1,500, **moderate** from 800, **weak** below 800.
**Consumer** — real (inflation-adjusted) retail sales against a year earlier, in percent: **healthy** from 3, **slowing** from 0, **contraction** below 0.

**Employment** — the month's change in nonfarm payrolls, in thousands of jobs: **strong** from 200, **moderate** from 75, **slowing** from 0, **contraction** below 0 — unless the Sahm rule indicator has reached 0.5, which overrides them all with **recession confirmed**.
**GDP** — real GDP growth in the latest quarter, at an annual rate, in percent: **strong** from 3, **moderate** from 1, **stall speed** from 0, **recession** below 0.

**Capex** — new orders for core capital goods (non-defence, excluding aircraft), the last three months against the three before, in percent: **expanding** from 3, **stable** from 0, **slowing** from −3, **warning** below −3.

**Consumer sentiment** — the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index, read the contrary way: **near bottom** below 60 carries a tick and counts slightly in growth's favour, **complacency** above 100 carries a warning triangle; otherwise **pessimistic** below 80, or **normal**.

blocks.text: How strong price pressure is. **Here a higher score means more inflation pressure.** Stance: **hot** at 0.40 or above (warning triangle), **moderate** in between (dash), **deflationary** at −0.40 or below (also a warning triangle). This card has no constructive stance, so its header never shows a tick. Weights: Core PCE and CPI 0.20 each, Oil and Wages 0.15 each, Core CPI, PPI and Copper 0.10 each; Shelter and the PPI CPI spread are shown for context and do not count.

Every value is the change against a year earlier, in percent, except Oil (dollars a barrel) and the PPI CPI spread (percentage points). Several labels are levels even though they sound like trends: CPI reads **rising** anywhere from 2.5% to 4%, whichever way it is moving.

items: **Core CPI** — consumer prices excluding food and energy: **hot** from 4, **above target** from 2.5, **at target** from 2, **below target** below 2.

**Core PCE** — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, excluding food and energy: **aggressive tightening** from 3, **hawkish bias** from 2.2, **at target** from 1.8, **below target** below 1.8. The labels name the policy response the level is associated with, not anything the Fed has done.
**CPI** — headline consumer prices: **hot** from 5, **above target** from 4, **rising** from 2.5, **goldilocks** from 1.5, **below target** from 0, **deflation risk** below 0.
**Shelter** — the housing component of CPI: **hot** from 5, **elevated** from 3.5, **moderating** from 2.5, **normalizing** below 2.5. Not scored.
**Oil** — WTI crude, in dollars a barrel: **inflationary risk** from 100, **elevated** from 80, **goldilocks** from 60, **low** from 50, **energy sector stress** below 50.
**PPI** — producer prices for final demand: **surge** from 8, **elevated** from 4, **moderate** from 2, **stable** from 0, **deflationary** below 0.

**PPI CPI spread** — PPI growth minus CPI growth: **margin pressure** from 3 (producers' prices rising faster than consumer prices), **margin expansion** at −3 or below, otherwise **neutral**. Not scored.
**Copper** — the copper price: **global expansion** from 10, **stable** from 0, **slowing** from −10, **global contraction** below −10.
**Wages** — average hourly earnings: **spiral risk** from 5, **elevated** from 4.5, **above target** from 3.5, **target consistent** from 2, **soft** below 2.

blocks.text: Stress from outside the US economy's own cycle: the dollar, the yen, China and US government borrowing. **Here too a higher score means more stress.** Stance: **elevated stress** at 0.35 or above (warning triangle), **moderate** in between (dash), **benign** at −0.15 or below (tick). Weights: Broad dollar and USD/JPY 0.28 each, China GDP 0.24 (not counted today, see below), Fiscal 0.20. Despite the card's name, no news or geopolitical-event data feeds it: every row is a FRED economic series.

items: **Broad dollar** — the Federal Reserve's trade-weighted index of the dollar against a broad basket of currencies, for goods trade; it is not the ICE dollar index (DXY) usually quoted. A stronger dollar reads as more stress: **major global stress** from 110, **EM commodity headwind** from 105, **neutral** from 100, **supportive equities** from 95, **dollar weak risk on** below 95.

**USD/JPY** — yen per US dollar. The label comes from its change over the last 22 daily readings (about a month), which is not shown: **systemic carry unwind** after a fall of 10% or more, **early carry unwind** after a fall of 5% or more, otherwise **carry intact**. A falling USD/JPY is a strengthening yen, which squeezes trades funded by borrowing in yen.

**China GDP** — reads **no recent data** and does not count. The app's series is the OECD's quarterly figure for China's GDP at current prices — nominal, not adjusted for inflation — compared with a year earlier, and it stopped updating after the third quarter of 2023. A reading whose newest observation is more than 270 days old (a quarterly series, dated at the start of its quarter and normally published months later) is treated as no recent data: it shows no value and is left out of the Global score.

**Fiscal** — the US federal deficit for the latest fiscal year as a share of GDP, in percent: **high deficit stress** above 6, **elevated supply risk** above 3 (more Treasury borrowing for markets to absorb), **manageable** up to 3. It sets a fiscal-year deficit against the latest quarter's annualised GDP, so it is approximate.

blocks.text: Despite its name, this card computes no statistical correlation — the measured correlations are under Seasonality & cycle context. It reads the four stances together with seven of their rows (Yield curve, Real rate, Credit spread, GDP, Oil, Broad dollar and USD/JPY) and shows the first pattern in a fixed list that fits. **Details** opens a one-line description of what that pattern matched and the **flags** that are on. The score is fixed for each regime: it says which pattern matched, not how strongly. The patterns, in the order they are checked:

items: **recession pipeline** (score −0.82, warning triangle) — Yield curve inverted or re steepening, Credit spread elevated or crisis, and weak growth: GDP stall speed or recession, or the Growth stance contraction.
**stagflation risk** (−0.58, warning triangle) — Inflation hot while Growth reads slowdown or contraction.
**rising inflation tight policy** (−0.48, warning triangle) — Inflation hot, Monetary Policy restrictive and the Yield curve flat, inverted or re steepening.

**global liquidity stress** (−0.52, warning triangle) — Global/Geopolitical Stress elevated stress with a strong dollar (Broad dollar EM commodity headwind or major global stress) or USD/JPY systemic carry unwind.
**deflation risk** (−0.18, warning triangle) — Inflation deflationary.
**goldilocks light** (+0.48, tick) — Inflation moderate, Monetary Policy accommodative or neutral, Growth expansion, and Credit spread neither elevated nor crisis.

**disinflation soft landing** (+0.32, tick) — Inflation not hot, Growth expansion, Monetary Policy not restrictive, Credit spread neither elevated nor crisis. Because goldilocks light is checked first, this is reached only when the Inflation or Monetary Policy stance has no reading.
**neutral mixed** (0, dash) — none of the above.

blocks.text: The flags are set independently of the regime:

items: **real rates headwind** — Real rate reads headwind.
**curve flat or inverted** — Yield curve flat, inverted or re steepening.
**credit stress** — Credit spread elevated or crisis.
**inflation hot** — the Inflation stance is hot.
**growth soft** — the Growth stance is slowdown or contraction.
**USD strong EM headwind** — Broad dollar EM commodity headwind or major global stress.
**global stress** — the Global/Geopolitical Stress stance is elevated stress.
**JPY carry stress** — USD/JPY systemic carry unwind.
**energy price pressure** — Oil elevated, inflationary risk or energy sector stress. Energy sector stress is oil below $50 a barrel, so a low oil price raises this flag too.

blocks.text: This card bundles two different things. Its header — a phase code, a score and a one-line description — is the **composite**, a market-wide reading that combines SPY's price picture with the four stances. **Inputs & index** opens what it was built from: **Blended inputs**, the four stance words it used (Growth, Policy, Inflation, Global), each with the icon stored for that word, and **Index**, the plain price facts of a single instrument, SPY (the fund that tracks the S&P 500). The Index facts describe SPY alone, carry no icon, and are the same numbers as SPY's card under Tracked.

**Index** lists **Symbol**; **Price phase**, by the rules below; **Drawdown**, how far the latest close is below the highest high of the last 252 sessions; **vs 200DMA**, that close against the average close of the last 200 sessions; **SMA200**, that average; **Close**; and **Crash warning**, yes or no.

The price phase is checked in this order: **crash** when the close is 12% or more below the highest high of the last 10 sessions, or 10% or more below the close 5 sessions earlier (the same test sets Crash warning); **bear** at a drawdown of −20% or worse; **correction** at −10% or worse; **pullback** at −3% or worse; then **bull extended** at 5% or more above the 200-session average, **bull** at or above it, **below 200-day average** below it. With fewer than 200 daily bars it is **insufficient data**. Because drawdown is checked first, an instrument 20% below its one-year high reads bear even while it is far above its 200-session average. Stock Detail's Price phase uses the same rules.
The composite is not an average. The price phase decides first; the stances only choose the code above the 200-session average, and elsewhere they nudge the score:

items: **crash panic** (score −0.95, warning triangle) — price phase crash, whatever the stances.
**bear structural** (−0.78, warning triangle) — price phase bear, whatever the stances.
**correction risk** (warning triangle) — price phase correction. Score −0.45, lowered by 0.10 when Inflation is hot and by 0.08 when Policy is restrictive.
**pullback healthy** (dash) — price phase pullback. Score −0.12, raised by 0.08 when Growth is expansion or slowdown, lowered by 0.05 when Inflation is hot.
**late cycle stretched** (0.15, dash) — price phase bull extended, with Inflation hot and Policy restrictive or neutral.
**bull fragile global** (0.22, dash) — bull extended otherwise, with Global elevated stress or moderate.
**bull overextended** (0.48, dash) — bull extended with neither.
**trend soft** (warning triangle) — price phase below 200-day average. Score −0.18, lowered by 0.20 when Growth is contraction.

**neutral mixed** (dash) — price phase bull. The score starts at 0.35 and moves with the stances: Growth expansion +0.12, slowdown +0.02, contraction −0.25; Inflation hot −0.08; Policy accommodative +0.05, restrictive −0.06. Two more codes belong to this branch — **bull macro aligned** (tick) above 0.55 and **bull macro divergent** (warning triangle) below −0.35 — but those adjustments can only move the score between −0.04 and 0.52, so as the rules stand a bull phase always reads neutral mixed and this card never shows a tick.
**insufficient equity data** (0, dashed circle) — fewer than 200 daily bars of SPY stored.

blocks.text: The score says which branch applied; it measures nothing further. The one-line description under the header says which branch matched — for example "Price phase bull extended, with the Inflation stance hot and Monetary Policy restrictive or neutral." — and is the same every time that code appears. It states what the rules found, not what to do about it. The as-of date is the day the composite was computed, not the date of SPY's close, which SPY's own card shows.

**Tracked** is a fixed list of eight: S&P 500 (SPY), Gold (GLD), Oil (WTI) (USO), the US 10-, 5- and 2-year Treasury yields (DGS10, DGS5, DGS2), Shell (SHEL) and Bitcoin (BTCUSDT). SPY, GLD and USO are exchange-traded funds, so their prices are fund share prices: Oil (WTI) is the USO fund's price, not dollars a barrel — the barrel price is the Oil row on the Inflation card. **Watchlist** lists each symbol on your Watchlist that is not already tracked, under its company name, or reads "No symbols on your watchlist."

A priced instrument shows its latest daily close, the change from the close before it (green for a rise, red for a fall) and that bar's date. "Today's session still forming" means the newest bar is today's and the New York session has not yet closed at 4 pm New York time, so that price is still moving. Below come its market-cycle facts: **Market-cycle phase** (the price-phase rules in the Market Cycle entry, applied to this instrument alone — no macro input), **Drawdown from peak**, **vs 200-day average**, a "Crash-velocity flag set" line when the crash test fired, and a **Basis** line with the date of the bars they were computed from and the windows used. The phase is shown as its stored code with the underscores as spaces, for example bull extended; below_sma reads below 200-day average.

For stocks and funds the windows are trading sessions — "Windows: peak lookback 252 · crash 10/5 · SMA 200": a one-year peak, crash tests over 10 and 5 sessions, and a 200-session average. Bitcoin trades every day, so its windows are calendar days (365, 14/7 and 200) and its prices are daily candles that close at 00:00 UTC, closed candles only ("Basis: 00:00 UTC daily close (closed candles only)"); its date can therefore differ from the stock market's.

The market-cycle facts come from the macro pass's last run and the price from the latest stored bar, so their dates can differ; each line carries its own. With fewer than 200 daily bars stored there is no phase, and the card says so in a line such as "154 1Day bars stored for …; need at least 200" (1Day is the app's name for daily bars). A newly added Watchlist symbol has no market-cycle reading until the next run, and its card says that too.

The three Treasury yields show only the yield, in percent, and its date. They have no phase by design: the phase rules are written for prices, and a yield is an interest rate — a yield falling from its high means bond prices rising, the opposite of a drawdown.

On a stock's or fund's card — SPY, GLD, USO, SHEL and your Watchlist symbols — the symbol next to the name opens its Stock Detail page, and **← Back to Daily Market Report** there returns here. The Treasury yields and Bitcoin have no Stock Detail page, so their symbols are plain text.

The panel is labelled "Static reference, not predictive." Its first two tiles come from fixed tables in the app, not from market data, and nothing in the panel feeds any stance, score or phase on the page.

items: **Month seasonality** — the current month (by UTC date), the table's tilt for it and the average S&P 500 monthly return the table quotes, for example "September · weak bear · historical average ~−0.7%", with a one-line note and the line "A fixed reference table, not computed from market data; no reading on this page uses it." From most to least favourable the tilts are strong bull (April, November, December), mild bull (January, March, July, October), neutral (February, May, June), mild bear (August) and weak bear (September): despite its name, weak bear is the most negative. The averages are the reference table's figures, not computed from the app's own price history.

**Presidential cycle** — the year of the US presidential term, counted from the calendar year with 2021 as year 1: Year 1 · post election · moderate constructive, Year 2 · midterm · choppy, Year 3 · pre election · strong historical, Year 4 · election · positive volatile, each with the table's one-line note.

blocks.text: **Intermarket correlations (60-day ρ vs equity)** are the app's measured correlations. Each row gives ρ, the correlation from −1 to +1 between SPY's daily return and the daily change in a second series over the latest 60 sessions (the second series' values are carried forward onto SPY's trading days), then the label for that ρ and a one-line description of what the label means. With fewer than 40 usable days a row reads insufficient data.

items: **VIX vs equity (60d)** — against the change in the VIX: **typical fear greed** at −0.25 or below (stocks rising as expected volatility falls), **unusual positive** at 0.15 or above, **compressed link** in between.

**Oil vs equity (60d)** — against the change in the WTI oil price: **procyclical** at 0.25 or above, **decoupled** at −0.25 or below, **neutral mixed** in between. Despite its name, decoupled means a clear negative link — stocks and oil moving in opposite directions — not the absence of one.

**Bond vs equity (60d)** — against the daily change in the price of a 10-year Treasury bond, stood in for by the 10-year yield with its sign reversed: a bond's price moves opposite to its yield. **deflationary hedge** at −0.25 or below means bond prices and stocks moved in opposite directions — bonds tended to rise on the days stocks fell; **inflationary positive** at 0.25 or above means they moved together, as when rising interest rates push both down; **transition neutral** in between. The label describes the last 60 sessions, not whether bonds will cushion a future fall.

**Economic calendar** — scheduled economic releases in the next 14 days, grouped by date, each with its time (your local time), country, name, impact and the actual, estimated and previous figures when known. "Economic calendar unavailable" means no events are stored for those 14 days; when none at all have been stored in the last 30 days, a note gives the known cause. At present the provider (Finnhub) refuses the request on the app's current plan, so this block is empty in every report: a data gap, not a quiet fortnight.

**Earnings (next 14 days)** — one line per stock on the page: Shell and each Watchlist symbol (funds, yields and Bitcoin report no earnings). It shows the date, quarter and the provider's time-of-day code (for example BMO, before the open, or AMC, after the close) when a date falls in the window; "No earnings date in the next 14 days." when the symbol is on the list the app fetches earnings dates for and no date in the window is stored; or "Earnings data not available for this symbol — data-macro-intel does not fetch it." when it is not on that list (data-macro-intel is the app's service that collects calendars and headlines). The last means missing data, not that no report is coming.

**News** — the eight newest market-wide headlines the app has collected, newest first, each as its title linked to the article (it opens in a new tab), followed by the stored name of the feed it came from — at present always finnhub_macro_general, Finnhub's general market-news feed. There is no article text — the app stores and shows only the headline, the feed and the link, as a copyright practice — no publication time and no sentiment score. The feed stores an article again each time it fetches it; the list shows each link once, at its newest copy, though the same story from different outlets can still appear more than once. These headlines are not tied to any symbol; they are the market-wide headlines that Stock Detail's Sentiment & news entry points to.

blocks.text: The footer lists the analysis areas in the app's reference material and how far each is built, then the known data gaps. It reads like a list of faults, but it is a disclosure: it states plainly what this report does not cover, so that a missing area is not mistaken for a quiet reading. Each line is the area, its status and a short note; the statuses are fixed text in the app, not live checks.

items: **partial** — partly covered elsewhere in the app, with no pipeline of its own (factor: quality and value overlap the fundamentals analysis, momentum and volatility come from price data).
**partial live** — part of it is computed live and the rest exists only as reference (intermarket: the three correlations above are live).
**live static** — on every report, but read from a fixed table rather than computed from data (seasonality and the presidential cycle).
**needs data** — would need data feeds the app does not have (sentiment: put/call ratios, options skew, short interest, margin; flow microstructure: options flow, dark pools).
**not automated** — not built (event driven, relative value, alternative data).

blocks.text: Below the list, each known data gap is stated with its cause — at present that the geopolitical risk index (GPR) is not ingested because its source is not configured, and why the economic calendar is empty. A gap line appears only while that gap exists.

sections.title: Today's Candidates (Momentum Scanner)
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* Today's Candidates is a screener. Once per trading session, after the US close, the scanner checks every eligible US common stock against six fixed rules — the gates — and lists the ones that passed all six, split into a market bucket and a penny bucket. It narrows roughly five thousand stocks to a short, reviewable list of unusual moves on unusual volume. It does not rank them by how likely they are to keep going, and nothing on this page is a forecast.

entries.title: What this page claims — and does not

blocks.text: Every candidate on this page met the published gates. That is the whole claim: none of the columns, and not the score, has been shown to predict what happens next.

A gate is a pass/fail rule. A stock must pass **all six** gates on the session's closing data to appear on the list. Failing any one gate **excludes** it — it is not listed with a low score, it is not listed at all. Scoring only ever happens among stocks that have already passed.

Stocks are judged in one of two **buckets**, decided by closing **price**, not by company size: **market** (closing at $2.00 or more) and **penny** ($0.30 to $2.00). The two buckets use the same six gates with different thresholds. Stocks under $0.30 are not judged at all, because at those prices ticks and reverse splits dominate the numbers.

On a stock's detail page you can see a partial pass — for example "Failed 3 of 6 gates" — with each gate's actual value next to its threshold. That is how a stock that is not on today's list explains itself.

entries.title: The six gates, one by one

items: **Price** — market: at least $2.00; penny: $0.30 to $2.00. This is also what decides the bucket.
**History** — at least 252 daily bars (about a year of trading), so that the 52-week measures below always have a full window.

**Day change** — market: up +8% to +25% on the day; penny: up +10% to +40%. The upper bound is deliberate: the scanner is built to notice a move early, and a stock already up +60% today is past that point. The bound stops the list from filling with moves that have already happened.
**Relative volume (RVOL)** — market: at least 3.0× its usual volume; penny: at least 4.0×. A price move on ordinary volume is not what this screener looks for.

**Dollar volume** — market: at least $5 million traded; penny: at least $2 million. Without this, the penny bucket fills with stocks so thinly traded that a small order moves the price and the RVOL figure means little.
**Market cap** — market: $300 million to $10 billion; penny: $300 million or less. This is a size check inside the price-decided bucket; it does not change which bucket a stock is in.

blocks.text: All thresholds are published defaults of the scanner, and every one of them is applied to the session's closing data only.

**RVOL** is today's volume divided by the stock's average daily volume over the previous 20 sessions — today excluded, so an unusual day cannot inflate its own baseline. 3.0× means three times the usual volume. If fewer than 20 prior sessions exist, RVOL is blank and the stock fails the RVOL gate rather than being given a made-up value. The list is sorted by RVOL by default because it describes *how unusual* today was, which is what a screener is for — not because a higher RVOL has been shown to predict a better outcome (it has not; see Backtest Lab).

**Dollar volume** is the closing price times the day's share volume: roughly how much money changed hands in the stock that session. It is a liquidity check — a stock can have huge RVOL on a few thousand dollars of trading, and dollar volume is what screens that out.

**RSI(14)** is the standard 14-session Relative Strength Index (see MasterClass, Module 3, for what it is in general). On this list it is **not** a reason a stock scores higher. A stock breaking out on heavy volume is *expected* to show a high RSI, so rewarding RSI would reward exactly what every candidate already has, and rewarding a low RSI would select against the moves the screener is looking for. RSI is used only as a **penalty**: above 85, the score loses 5 points as "exhausted momentum". Otherwise it is shown for information.
**Breakout State** describes where today's close sits against the stock's highest high of the previous 20 sessions (today excluded), judged on the close, never on an intraday spike:

items: **breakout_from_consolidation** — closed above that 20-session high after a quiet stretch (the prior 20 sessions' range was under 25% of the price).
**breakout** — closed above that high without the quiet stretch before it.
**approaching** — closed within 2% below that high.
**none** — anything else.

blocks.text: What testing found

This field was tested for one question: does it help predict which candidates go on to rise **100% or more within 120 sessions**? In the original check on 218 candidates, the stocks in the stronger-breakout half reached +100% far *less* often than the weaker half (8 against 26 hits) — the field measured **inverted**. That is why its weight in the score was set to **zero**: it once earned up to 20 points, and now earns none.

A larger follow-up on 6,924 candidate episodes sharpened the picture instead of simply repeating it. **breakout_from_consolidation**, the most common state, reached +100% just 6.42% of the time, against 15.57% for **none**. But a plain **breakout** was the best state in that sample at 20.89%, above the 10.53% average. So "inverted" is true of the field as it was scored, and of its most common value — not of every value. One weight cannot fit both, which is a design finding, not a tuning one.

The likely reading is lateness: among stocks that have already passed the gates, a fresh breakout often marks a move further along, with less room left to run. Both checks were made on the scanner's earlier candidate definition and have not been repeated since. The field is still computed and shown because it describes the chart, and because it is informative in other ways — it simply does not add to the score.

**52-Week High %** is today's close divided by the highest high of the previous 251 sessions (today excluded). 100% means the stock closed exactly at its prior 52-week high; above 100% means today set a **new** 52-week high.
What testing found

Tested for the same question — reaching **+100% within 120 sessions** — it also measured **inverted**. In the original check on 218 candidates, the half nearer its 52-week high reached +100% less often (10 against 24 hits). In the 6,924-episode follow-up, candidates above the median reached +100% 6.70% of the time against 14.36% below it: a gap of 7.65 percentage points, far too large to be chance. Unlike Breakout State, this one held cleanly in both checks.

That is why its weight is **zero**. It once earned up to 5 points, the most of all for a fresh 52-week high — which is precisely the case that measured backwards. The reading is the same lateness: among stocks that have already passed the gates, being at a new high marks a move further along, not a better one. Both checks were made on the scanner's earlier candidate definition and have not been repeated since. The field is still computed and shown, because it describes where the price is.

**Catalyst Tier** is meant to say whether company news explains the move: **A** (strong news such as an approval, acquisition, major contract or raised guidance), **B** (weaker news such as an analyst upgrade or a partnership), or **none** (the stock was checked and there was no company news in the last 48 hours). A blank means the stock was **not checked** — and today that is every stock, because the news classifier is not yet running on live data. A blank is therefore missing information, not a sign that nothing happened; the detail page says "Not checked — catalyst data not yet ingested".

**Market Cap** is the value the market-cap gate uses: the session's closing price times the company's most recent share count **filed with the SEC** on or before that day. It is the same definition the scanner's research used, so today's list is drawn the same way as the history that was tested. If the company has no such filing, or its latest one is **more than 15 months old** — too old to trust once shares have been issued or reverse-split since — the market cap counts as unavailable and the stock fails the gate. The scanner never fills the gap with an estimate. Some companies that still file are excluded this way because their recent filings are missing from the scanner's data; that is a known gap, not a judgement about the company.

The **score** is a 0–100 research number computed only for stocks that passed the gates. It adds up weighted parts: relative volume (up to 35), volume acceleration (25), catalyst (15), estimated float (10), and trading above the 20-day volume-weighted average price (5). Breakout State and 52-Week High % are weighted **zero** because they measured inverted. Ten points are deliberately left unassigned, so the most any stock can reach is 90. Penalties then subtract points for exhausted momentum (RSI above 85), an already-extended day (up more than 20%), and volume that is high but already fading.

Each score is shown against **its own ceiling**, e.g. **53/75** rather than 53: the ceiling is 90 minus the weight of every part that is missing for that stock. With the catalyst part blank for every stock today, the ceiling is 75. Showing "/75" stops a 53 from reading as "53 out of 100".
The score is always labelled **unvalidated**, everywhere it appears:

The header reads, for example, "4,967 of 5,000 symbols scanned". **Eligible** is the list of stocks the scanner is meant to cover: common stock on NASDAQ, NYSE or NYSE American — no ETFs, funds, warrants, units, preferred shares, ADRs or REITs. **Scanned** is how many of them actually got a result for this session. The two differ when a stock's data is not available for that day — for example a missing daily bar — so it could not be evaluated. A stock that was not scanned is simply absent; it has not been judged and failed.

entries.title: Scan date and a stale scan

blocks.text: The **scan date** is the trading session the list covers. The scanner runs after the close, so each morning the list shows the previous session. The scan is **stale** when a newer session should exist by now — its 4:00 pm New York close plus a six-hour grace period has passed, on the NYSE's own trading calendar with its holidays — but no scan for it has been stored. Weekends and market holidays never make it stale. When it is stale, the page keeps showing the older, still-correct list and says so above it: "Couldn't load today's results — showing the scan from …".

Every column can be sorted, the score included, and the list opens sorted by RVOL. The sort line always says what it is — "Sorted by RVOL — descriptive, not predictive" — because reordering a list is not the same as ranking candidates by how good they are. That is why the "unvalidated" label stays next to the score in every row and every sort order: sorting by score puts the highest numbers on top, but those numbers have not been shown to predict anything, so the top of that list is not "the best" candidates.

sections.title: Stock Detail — full analysis
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* Stock Detail is the full picture of one symbol. For a symbol the scanner covers, the top of the page shows which of the scanner's gates it passed or failed, its primary facts, and its score, marked unvalidated; a symbol the scanner has never covered shows "No scanner data for this symbol" there instead, and everything below still works. Below that comes the full analysis — technical readings, fundamentals, balance sheet, cash flow, correlations, news, qualitative signals, and context against the market benchmark (SPY) — each a plain, neutral reading of stored data, not a signal. The first time a symbol's analysis is opened it may take a few seconds to compute, and the page says so instead of showing a spinner. Last comes Classical Technical Signals, the one section with its own accent colour, because it is pattern-matching rather than a reading of data; its entry below explains what it shows and what testing found.

entries.title: The top of the page: date, candidacy and gates

blocks.text: The header shows the symbol and the date its data is **as of**, always "after market close": everything on this page comes from one session's closing data, never from the live market.

If the symbol is not on today's list, a notice says so and why — either it **didn't pass today's gates** (the gates panel shows which), or its latest data is **older than the latest scan**, because no newer daily bar has arrived for it yet. A symbol that passed on an older date is never presented as a candidate today.

The **gates panel** reads either "Passed the gates" or, for example, "Failed 3 of 6 gates", with the session date. Each of the six gates is listed with the symbol's actual value next to the bucket's threshold, a tick or a cross, and the scanner's own reason code for any failure. Pass or fail is read from what the scanner stored, never re-judged by the page; any reason code that doesn't belong to one of the six gates is listed separately rather than hidden.

A symbol that failed the gates has **no score** — the page says "No score" instead of showing a number. A symbol the scanner has never covered at all (for example an ETF, or a company outside the eligible list) shows "No scanner data for this symbol" in place of the gates, facts and score; the analysis sections below it still work.
One session's stored facts for the symbol, all from the daily close. Blank values show "—", never 0.

items: **Last close** — the session's closing price as traded, with the prior close beneath it.
**Day change** — the move from the prior close, in dollars and percent. It is the only fact coloured green or red, because it is a price move.
**Volume** and **Avg volume (20-day)** — today's shares traded, and the average of the previous 20 sessions (today excluded).
**Dollar volume** — closing price times volume; see the Today's Candidates entry.
**RVOL (20-day)** — today's volume divided by that 20-session average; see the Today's Candidates entry.

**Float shares (est.)** — the number of shares outstanding, used as a stand-in for the public float because free data sources do not provide true float. It is always an estimate and always marked "(est.)": insider and locked-up shares are not removed, so it overstates the float for recently listed and insider-heavy companies.
**RSI (14)** — the 14-session Relative Strength Index; here it only ever counts against the score (above 85).
**52-week high** — the highest high of the previous 251 sessions, with how far today's close sits from it.
**Breakout state** — where the close sits against the prior 20-session high; see the Today's Candidates entry and its testing result.
**Gap** — the session's opening price against the prior close: how far it opened up or down before trading.

**VWAP distance** — how far the close is above or below the **20-day** volume-weighted average price, computed from daily bars. It is not the intraday VWAP that trading platforms show for the current session.
**ATR %** — the 14-session average true range divided by the close: the stock's typical daily range as a share of its price, a plain measure of how volatile it has been.
**Market cap** — the value the market-cap gate used; see the Today's Candidates entry.

**Identified catalyst** — the company-news headline behind the catalyst tier, when one is found. Today it reads "Not checked — catalyst data not yet ingested" for every symbol, because the news classifier is not yet running on live data.

blocks.text: The chart's range buttons change which bars you see, and the caption under the chart always says which kind you are looking at:

items: **1D and 5D** — 5-minute bars from the regular session, in New York time, for the last one or five sessions. They are stored only for candidates and watchlist symbols. A symbol without them shows its last one or five **daily** bars instead, with the caption "No intraday data for … yet — showing daily bars" — never a single daily bar dressed up as an intraday chart.

**1M, 6M, 1Y and ALL** — daily bars, adjusted for splits and dividends ("Daily bars · split/dividend adjusted"), so a past split does not show as a sudden crash. The window ends at the symbol's latest daily bar, so a symbol whose data is a few days old still shows a full window.

blocks.text: Intraday bars are shown as traded, not adjusted; the daily ranges are adjusted. That is why a price on the 5D chart and the same day on the 1Y chart can differ slightly after a dividend or split.

Shown only for a symbol that passed the gates. The top line is the **total**, and three numbers sit together: the **total**, the **attainable** ceiling for this symbol, and the **allocated** maximum of 90. Ninety because ten of the score's 100 points are deliberately left unassigned; attainable because any part with a missing input scores 0 and cannot be earned — today the catalyst part is blank for every symbol, so attainable is 75. A total always reads against its own ceiling, e.g. 53 of 75, never out of 100.

Each part is listed as points earned against its maximum — relative volume up to 35, volume acceleration 25, catalyst 15, float 10, VWAP 5 — and **breakout** and **52-week high** at a maximum of **0**. Those two were zeroed because they measured *inverted*: among stocks that passed the gates, stronger readings were followed by fewer big moves, not more (see their Today's Candidates entries). They are still listed, at 0, so the breakdown shows where they went.

**Missing inputs (scored 0)** lists every part that had no data, so a low total can be told apart from missing information. **Penalties** lists all three rules every time, fired or not — RSI above 85 (exhausted momentum, −5), day change above 20% (already extended, −10), and volume that is high but fading (RVOL 3 or more while volume acceleration is below 1.0, −5) — so a rule that didn't fire shows as checked and zero rather than absent.
Why the score is marked unvalidated

In plain terms: the score was tested for whether higher-scoring candidates reached **+100% within 120 sessions** more often than lower-scoring ones in the same bucket. They did not — within the penny bucket and within the market bucket, higher and lower scores did no better than each other, which is what the p-values in the note say. An earlier result that pooled both buckets looked positive, but 97% of it was explained by which bucket the candidates came from, not by the score. The score is kept as a research baseline, not as a ranking.

The **Technical analysis** card shows ten readings computed from the symbol's daily bars, for the session named in its header ("· stale" is added when a newer daily bar has arrived since they were computed). Each is a plain description of the chart, with the band the app puts it in: none of them is a signal, and the score does not use them. Readings that currently carry a flag — RSI outside its normal band, an active squeeze, or VIX above 25 — are not marked here; they are listed once, with their badge, under Classical Technical Signals. For what RSI and MACD are in general, see MasterClass, Module 3.

items: **RSI (14)** — the 14-session Relative Strength Index of daily closes, with its band: **oversold** below 30, **overbought** above 70, **normal** from 30 to 70 (both included). These are the lines the analyst bot's RSI alerts use. The score's separate RSI rule — a penalty above 85 — is described under Today's Candidates. It is computed separately from the RSI (14) in Primary facts, over a different stretch of stored price history, so the two can differ slightly.

**MACD histogram** — the MACD line (the 12-session minus the 26-session exponential moving average of closes) minus its 9-session signal line: positive when the MACD line is above its signal line, negative when below. "Bullish cross" or "Bearish cross" appears beneath it only on the session the MACD line crossed its signal line, upward or downward; on any other session there is no line.

**ADX (14)** — the 14-session Average Directional Index: how strong the trend is, **not which way** it runs — a steady fall reads as high as a steady rise. The band is **strong trend** above 25 and **not strong trend** at 25 or below. There is no "weak" band, because 25 is the only ADX threshold the app's rules use.

**Trend** — **Up**, **Down** or **Sideways** over the last 60 sessions. The window is split in half: if the second half made both a higher high and a higher low than the first, it reads Up; if it made neither, Down. If it made one but not the other, a straight line fitted through the 60 closes decides — but only when the fit is reasonably tight (R² of 0.3 or more); otherwise it reads Sideways. **Slope** beneath is that line's gradient as a percentage of the average close, **per session**: 0.07% means the fitted line rises by about 0.07% of the price each trading day.

**MA cross** — **Golden cross** when the 50-session simple moving average of closes moved above the 200-session one on this session, **Death cross** when it moved below. It marks only the session the cross happens, so on nearly every day it shows "—": no cross that session, not missing data (it is also "—" for a symbol with fewer than 202 daily bars). It does not say which average is currently on top.

**ATR (14)** — the 14-session Average True Range, in dollars: the stock's typical daily range, counting any gap from the prior close. ATR % in Primary facts is the same kind of measure divided by the close.

**BB squeeze** — **Active** when, on the latest session, the Bollinger Bands (the 20-session average of closes ± 2 standard deviations) sit entirely inside the Keltner Channel (the 20-session exponential average of closes ± 2 × the 10-session ATR); otherwise **Not active**. It describes a quiet, compressed stretch, and it is common. What testing found about squeezes is under Classical Technical Signals.

**VIX regime** — the CBOE Volatility Index, a market-wide measure of the S&P 500 volatility expected over the next 30 days. It is not a reading of this stock, and it is the same for every symbol. It is the newest daily VIX close the app had stored (from FRED) when the readings were computed, so it can be a day or more older than the session in the header. Bands: **extreme fear** above 35, **elevated** above 20 up to 35, **normal** from 12 to 20, **complacency** below 12. The Daily Market Report bands VIX with the same thresholds. **Elevated** is a label, not a warning: the analyst bot's VIX alert fires only above 25, and only above 25 is VIX listed as a flagged reading under Classical Technical Signals.

**Pivot (prior bar)** — classic pivot levels from the **previous** session's high, low and close: pivot (PP) = (high + low + close) ÷ 3, R1 = 2 × PP − low, S1 = 2 × PP − high. Because this page is as of the latest close, they are the levels for the session that just closed, worked out from the one before it — not levels for the next session.

**SMC counts** — three counts from the "Smart Money Concepts" style of chart reading, shown as, for example, "3 FVG · 5 OB · 3 sweeps". **FVG** (fair value gaps): three-bar gaps — a bar's low above the high of the bar two sessions earlier, or its high below that bar's low, by at least 0.1% — found in the last 50 sessions that no later bar has traded back into. **OB** (order blocks): in the last 100 sessions, the last down-candle before a swing low that was followed by a rise of at least 1.5% (or the last up-candle before a swing high followed by a fall of at least 1.5%), not closed through since. **Sweeps**: sessions in the last 50 whose high went above the most recent swing high but closed back below it, or whose low went below the most recent swing low but closed back above it; every such session in the window counts, not only recent ones. A swing high or low here is a bar higher (or lower) than the three bars on each side of it. The order-block and sweep counts feed the action signal in Classical Technical Signals; the FVG count does not. What testing found is in that entry.

blocks.text: The **Fundamentals** card shows the company's financial figures and the tier the app puts each one in. The figures come from the app's fundamentals data provider, and the header says when they were **computed** ("· stale" is added when newer raw figures have arrived since, or the computation has passed its maximum age). The app stores reported financial statements and earnings history for the equities on **Followed Symbols** and for every equity it currently computes for another reason — on your Watchlist, one of today's candidates, or a Compute request (see **Computed Symbols**); for any other symbol it has only the provider's summary figures, so fields that need the statements show "—". "—" always means not available, never zero.

**Composite** is the average of whichever tiered readings are available, each scored +1 for its best tier, 0 for its middle tier, and −0.5 or −1 for its worst: EPS strength, Revenue, the P/E band, FCF yield, Gross margin, Net margin, and PEG. It runs from −1 to +1 and reads **strong** at 0.5 or above, **weak** at −0.5 or below, and **neutral** in between. Because only the available readings count, one symbol's composite can rest on four readings and another's on seven. PEG counts toward it whenever the provider supplies one, even though the PEG cell itself shows "—".

items: **EPS strength** — growth in earnings per share over the last twelve months against the twelve months before: **strong** at 15% or more, **neutral** from 5% up to 15%, **weak** below 5% (including any decline). When the provider has no growth figure, it falls back to whether trailing EPS is positive: positive reads **neutral**; zero or negative reads **weak**.

**Revenue** — revenue growth on the same basis: **strong** at 10% or more, **neutral** from 2% up to 10%, **weak** below 2%. It includes growth that came from acquisitions; organic growth is not available.

**P/E band (trailing)** — a band on the company's trailing twelve-month P/E: **value** under 15, **growth fair** from 15 up to 25, **expensive** at 25 or more, and **loss making** when the P/E is zero or negative. The data provider supplies no genuine five-year average P/E, so the page makes no comparison with the company's own history.

**FCF yield** — free cash flow (cash from operations minus capital spending) from the company's latest annual report, divided by market cap: **attractive** at 5% or more, **fair** from 2% up to 5%, **avoid** below 2%, including negative free cash flow. It needs reported financial statements, so it shows only for symbols with stored statements, and because it uses the latest annual report rather than the last twelve months it can be up to a year behind.

**Gross margin** — gross profit as a share of revenue over the last twelve months: **high** at 40% or more, **average** from 20% up to 40%, **margin pressure** below 20%. Normal gross margins differ widely between industries, and the band does not adjust for that.
**Net margin** — net income as a share of revenue over the last twelve months: **strong** at 15% or more, **average** from 5% up to 15%, **pressure** below 5% (including losses).

**Trend** (beneath Gross and Net margin) — **expanding**, **stable** or **compressing**: the margin across the company's latest eight quarterly reports (at least four are needed), comparing the average of the two newest with the two oldest. More than 2 percentage points up reads expanding, more than 2 down compressing. Only symbols with stored statements have it.

**PEG** — always "—", with the note "Not served by the analysis API". The app does store a PEG ratio (P/E divided by earnings growth) for the symbols whose provider supplies one, and it counts toward the composite — **undervalued growth** below 1, **fairly valued growth** from 1 up to 2, **expensive growth** at 2 or more — but this page does not show it yet.

**Earnings surprise** — always "—", with the same note. For symbols with stored earnings history the app does compute an average earnings surprise — how far reported EPS beat or missed analysts' estimates, averaged over up to the last four quarters — but this page does not show it yet, and it does not count toward the composite.
**TTM P/E** — the trailing twelve-month price-to-earnings ratio as supplied by the provider: the same number the P/E band is judged on. "—" when the provider has no P/E for the company.

**Market cap** — the provider's latest market capitalisation for the company. It is not the value the scanner's market-cap gate uses (see the Today's Candidates entry), so the two can differ. It shows "—" when the provider reports it in a currency other than the US dollar — for example companies listed in Toronto, London, Tel Aviv or Taiwan — rather than a wrongly converted figure.

blocks.text: The **Balance sheet** card shows how much profit the company makes on its capital, how much it owes, and whether it can cover its short-term bills, each with the tier the app puts it in. It has no date line of its own: it is computed together with the Fundamentals card, at the time shown there, and the same limit applies — for a symbol without stored financial statements, figures that need them show "—".

**Composite** averages four tiered readings — ROE, ROIC, Debt / equity and Current ratio — each scored +1 for its best tier, 0 for its middle tier and −1 for its worst. It reads **healthy** at 0.5 or above, **stressed** at −0.5 or below, and **neutral** in between. Only available readings count: today ROIC and Debt / equity come only from reported statements, so for a symbol without stored statements the composite rests on ROE and Current ratio alone. ROA, Quick ratio and Net debt / operating income are shown but do not count.

items: **ROE** — return on equity: net income over the last twelve months as a share of shareholders' equity. **excellent** at 15% or more, **adequate** from 8% up to 15%, **low** below 8%.

**ROA** — return on assets: net income over the last twelve months as a share of total assets, i.e. how much profit the company makes from everything it owns. **high** at 10% or more, **moderate** from 5% up to 10%, **low** below 5%. Shown for information; it does not count toward the composite.

**ROIC** — return on invested capital: one year's operating income from the latest annual report, after tax (the company's own effective rate when it is between 0 and 50%, otherwise 21%), divided by total assets minus current liabilities from the latest balance sheet. **high** at 15% or more, **adequate ROIC** from 8% up to 15%, **low ROIC** below 8%. It counts toward the composite.

**Current ratio** — current assets divided by current liabilities, from the latest reported quarter: whether what the company expects to turn into cash within a year covers what it must pay within a year. **safe** at 1.5 or more, **monitor** from 1.0 up to 1.5, **liquidity risk** below 1.0.

**Quick ratio** — like the current ratio, but leaving out inventory, which can be slow to turn into cash. **adequate** at 1.0 or more, **monitor** from 0.7 up to 1.0, **low** below 0.7. Shown for information; it does not count toward the composite.

**Debt / equity** — total debt divided by shareholders' equity, from the latest balance sheet: **conservative** below 1.0, **manageable** from 1.0 up to 2.0, **high leverage** at 2.0 or more. Normal leverage differs a great deal by industry (banks and utilities run higher safely). It counts toward the composite.

**Net debt / operating income** — total debt minus cash, from the latest balance sheet, divided by one year's operating income from the latest annual report: **net cash** below 0 (more cash than debt), **conservative** below 2, **manageable** from 2 up to 4, **high risk** at 4 or more. When operating income is zero or negative the ratio means nothing, and the cell reads **operating loss** instead. It is shown for information and does not count toward the composite.

blocks.text: The **Cash flow** card shows the company's latest **annual** cash-flow statement as filed. US companies file it in a 10-K, which the app reads through its filings provider, Finnhub, in US dollars. Foreign issuers listed in the US — such as TSMC (TSM), Shell (SHEL), TotalEnergies (TTE), BP and GlobalFoundries (GFS) — file a 20-F instead, which the app reads from SEC EDGAR's companyfacts data under the IFRS taxonomy. The header names the form, the fiscal year and its end, the filing date and the source exactly as the card shows it, for example "10-K · fiscal year 2025, ended 31 Dec 2025 · filed 18 Feb 2026 · 10-K via Finnhub" or "20-F · fiscal year 2024, ended 31 Dec 2024 · filed 17 Apr 2025 · 20-F via SEC EDGAR". It never shows a single quarter: the cash-flow figures in a quarterly report (10-Q) are totals for the fiscal year so far, not the quarter's own, so the card notes "Annual figures only — quarterly cash-flow figures are year-to-date."

Figures are shown in the filing's own reporting currency, named once in the header, and are never converted: "Figures in USD, as reported", or for another currency "Figures in TWD, as reported — not converted". TSMC reports in New Taiwan dollars, so its card reads in TWD; the US-dollar convenience figures its 20-F also contains are deliberately not used. US-dollar amounts are shortened as $51.97B; any other currency is written with its ISO code rather than a guessed symbol, for example TWD 1,826.18B.

items: **Net cash from operating activities**, **Net cash from investing activities** and **Net cash from financing activities** — the statement's three totals, as filed and shortened. A negative figure, shown with a minus sign, is cash that went out.

**Capital spending (property, plant & equipment)**, **Share buybacks** and **Dividends paid** — amounts the company paid, shown as positive figures and marked "amount paid". For a 20-F they are the statement's own lines for purchase of property, plant and equipment, repurchases of shares, and dividends paid to the parent company's shareholders.

A line with no figure shows "—", never zero, with the reason the app gives: "not in filing" when a 10-K does not contain it, or "not reported as a comparable line" when a 20-F filer reports that line under its own company-specific item, or folded into a broader line, instead of the standard one — so there is no like-for-like figure to show. Shell's and TotalEnergies' capital expenditure are their own items; BP's combines property, plant and equipment with intangible and other non-current assets.

blocks.text: SEC's companyfacts data can lag a newly filed 20-F. When SEC EDGAR lists a newer 20-F than the one shown, the card says so in one line, for example "A newer 20-F (fiscal year ended 31 Dec 2025, filed 16 Apr 2026) is on SEC EDGAR but not in its companyfacts data yet." — as for TSMC, whose card still shows fiscal year 2024.

These are plain facts from the filing: no tier and no green or red. When there is no statement the card still appears and says why, in a sentence starting "No cash-flow statement available:" — a crypto pair, a fund (funds file no company cash-flow statement), a listing outside the US (neither filings source covers it), a company for which Finnhub returned no 10-K or 10-Q and SEC EDGAR has no IFRS (20-F) cash-flow statement either, or a symbol whose filings have not been fetched yet (they are fetched once it is followed, on the Watchlist, a candidate, or computed).

The **Correlations** card checks whether figures that ought to agree actually do — for example, whether a low P/E comes with strong earnings growth, or heavy debt with thin margins. It reads the tiers already worked out for the Fundamentals and Balance sheet cards, plus a few the page does not show (interest coverage, free cash flow against net income, goodwill, price-to-book, capital spending and dividend yield). It is computed together with the Fundamentals card, at the time shown there, and the same limit applies: for a symbol without stored financial statements, most comparisons have nothing to compare. A figure the app cannot work out from the company's latest reports — for example interest coverage when the latest annual report has no interest-expense line — is left empty, and every comparison that needs it is skipped rather than run on an older figure. The score does not use this card.

Each **cluster** runs a handful of comparisons. A comparison that finds clear agreement adds a point, a clear conflict takes one away (a few count a half, one counts double), and one that finds neither counts as checked with 0. The cluster's score is its total divided by the number of comparisons that could be run, kept between −1 and +1, and **Cluster health** shows its band, for example "Earnings Quality — mostly agree": **mostly agree** at 0.5 or above, **mixed, leaning agree** from 0 up to 0.5, **mixed, leaning conflict** from −0.5 up to 0, **mostly conflict** below −0.5. A cluster in which no comparison could be run reads **not evaluated** — it has no score and no band. It is common, and for a symbol without stored financial statements it is the usual case. **Composite** is the plain average of the scores of the clusters that were evaluated, with the same bands — a cluster that was not evaluated is left out, not counted as 0, so with only one cluster evaluated the composite is that cluster's score. When no cluster was evaluated, Composite reads **not evaluated** too.
The four clusters

items: **Earnings Quality** — whether earnings, cash, revenue and margins move together. Four comparisons. EPS growth against **FCF yield** (free cash flow divided by the company's market value): EPS growth above 10% with an FCF yield below 2% conflicts; above 10% with a yield of 5% or more agrees. Because the yield divides by market value, a high share price alone can make it low, so this comparison conflicts for some large, cash-generating companies whose shares are highly valued. Revenue against EPS, judged on the Fundamentals card's Revenue and EPS strength: both **strong** agrees; strong EPS with **weak** revenue conflicts, and so (by half a point) does strong revenue with weak EPS. The gross margin trend against the net margin trend (the Fundamentals card's Trend): gross expanding with net compressing conflicts, both compressing conflicts, both expanding agrees. Revenue growth against the gross margin trend: growth of 10% or more with a compressing trend conflicts by half a point, and with a stable or expanding trend agrees; revenue shrinking with a compressing trend conflicts. The two trend comparisons run only when the trends exist (at least four quarterly reports).

**Valuation vs Quality** — whether the price paid matches the quality: a P/E above 25 with EPS growth below 5%, or with ROIC below 8%, conflicts; a P/E below 15 with EPS growth of 15% or more, or with ROIC of 15% or more, agrees. It also compares price-to-book with ROE (below 1.5× with ROE of 15% or more agrees; above 5× with ROE below 15% conflicts) and, when the dividend yield is above 2%, whether free cash flow covers it (a dividend yield above the FCF yield conflicts; an FCF yield at least 1.5 times the dividend yield agrees).

**Leverage & Liquidity** — whether the balance sheet can carry its debt. Net debt / operating income against interest coverage (one year's operating income divided by interest expense, from the latest annual report; left empty when that report has no interest-expense line): both at high risk — 4 or more, and under 2× — counts double against; either one alone counts against; conservative net debt (0 up to 2 — a company with more cash than debt does not count here) with coverage of 5× or more counts for. The current ratio against **FCF conversion** (free cash flow divided by net income, from the latest annual report, and only worked out when both are positive): below 1.0 with conversion under 0.7 against, 1.5 or more with conversion of 1.0 or more for. Debt / equity against net margin: 2.0 or more with a margin under 5% against, below 1.0 with 15% or more for. Goodwill and intangibles as a share of total assets against FCF conversion: 20% or more with conversion under 0.7 against, below 20% with 1.0 or more for.

**Operational** — whether growth earns its keep: ROIC below 8% with revenue growth of 10% or more conflicts; ROIC of 15% or more with that growth agrees, and with revenue growth below 2% agrees by half a point. The gross margin trend on its own: compressing conflicts, expanding agrees, stable counts as checked with 0. And capital spending as a share of revenue against FCF yield: under 5% with a yield of 5% or more agrees, over 20% with a yield under 2% conflicts.

blocks.text: Aligned and divergent signals

Every comparison that found agreement leaves a line under **Aligned signals**; every conflict leaves one under **Divergent signals** — all four clusters' lines together, in cluster order. When there are none, the card says "No aligned signals stored." or "No divergent signals stored."

Each line names the comparison that was met, for example "High debt / equity with a net margin of 3.1%" or "Gross margin trend compressing". **High**, **low**, **strong**, **weak** and **fast** refer to the bands described above, and a number in the line is the company's own figure. A line says which figures lined up or clashed; it does not say why, or what follows from it.
Combined patterns

The **Combined patterns** line reads, for example, "Net count: 0" or "Net count: −1 · met: strong EPS with weak cash signs". It comes from five fixed patterns, each a list of conditions; a pattern is **met** when enough of its conditions hold at once. Only the names of the patterns that were met are shown, not which conditions held.

items: **Low P/E with quality conditions** — at least 3 of 5: a P/E below 25; ROIC of 15% or more; free cash flow at least equal to net income, or an FCF yield of 5% or more; debt / equity below 1.0; and insider buying (Insider activity reads cluster buy or single buy). "Below 25" includes P/Es that the Fundamentals card bands as **growth fair**.

**Cash strength with flat EPS** — at least 2 of 3: EPS strength **neutral** or **weak**; free cash flow at least equal to net income; an FCF yield of 5% or more. The two cash conditions are enough on their own.

**Strong EPS with weak cash signs** — at least 2 of 3: EPS strength **strong**; the Earnings Quality comparison above finding EPS growth above 10% with an FCF yield below 2%, *and* cash that is weak against earnings — FCF conversion under 0.7, or negative free cash flow; accounts receivable growing faster than revenue between the last two annual reports, by a factor of more than 1.1 (for example receivables up 12% while revenue is flat). The cash test is there because FCF yield divides by market value: a low yield alone can come from a high share price, and does not count.
**Low P/E with weak conditions** — at least 3 of 4: a P/E below 25; ROIC below 15%; debt / equity of 1.0 or more; revenue growth below 2%. All four are levels at one point in time, not declines.
**Debt and liquidity strain** — at least 3 of 4: net debt / operating income of 4 or more; interest coverage under 2×; FCF conversion under 0.7; a current ratio below 1.0.

blocks.text: **Net count** is the number of the first two patterns met minus the number of the other three met: "+2 or more", "+1", "0", "−1" or "−2 or less". 0 is the usual reading, and it most often means that nothing was met. The app has not tested whether any of these patterns is followed by a particular price move: like the rest of the card, they describe how the company's reported figures relate to each other, not what the stock will do.
A symbol with no correlation data at all shows "No correlation clusters stored." and "Net count: —".

Despite its name, the **Sentiment & news** card shows no sentiment. It lists the symbol's newest stored headlines — up to ten, newest first, however old — each as its title, linked to the article, followed by the name of the feed it came from. There is no article text — the app stores and shows only the headline, the feed and the link, as a copyright practice — and no per-headline score; the sentiment readings, when there are any, are the News sentiment rows in the Qualitative signals card below.

Today it reads "No headlines stored for this symbol." for every symbol. Company headlines reach the app from two feeds: the Alpha Vantage news-sentiment download described under Qualitative signals, currently turned away by the provider's request limit, and a company-news feed that is not currently running. The market-wide headlines the app does collect are not tied to any symbol, so they appear in the Daily Market Report instead of here.

The **Qualitative signals** card holds five readings about the company beyond its financial ratios. Each shows its value with the app's band in brackets — for example "1.00 (3 of 3 conditions)" — or **Insufficient data** when the app looked and had too little to classify, or "—" when no reading is stored at all. It is computed together with the Fundamentals card, at the time shown there.

items: **Moat proxy** — a rough, numbers-only stand-in for a durable competitive advantage (a "moat"); it knows nothing of brands, patents or network effects. It gives a point for each of three: a gross margin of 40% or more (the provider's last-twelve-month figure, or without it the average of the quarterly margins below); a steady gross margin across the company's latest quarterly reports (up to eight, at least four needed), meaning a standard deviation under 5 percentage points; and return on equity of 15% or more over the last twelve months. Three points read **1.00 (3 of 3 conditions)**, two **0.50 (2 of 3 conditions)**, one or none **0.00 (0–1 of 3 conditions)**. A company with fewer than four quarterly reports that include both revenue and a gross-profit line reads **Insufficient data** — for several large companies the app's data has no separate gross-profit line at all; a symbol with no reported statements in the app's data shows "—".

**Insider activity** — share purchases and sales by company insiders (officers, directors and large holders), from the SEC Form 4 filings the app's data provider supplies. Since March 2026 the officers and directors of most foreign companies whose shares are registered in the US file Form 4 too (those of companies from some countries, such as the UK and Canada, are exempt), so such a company can have insider rows from that month on. They are collected only for the equities the app stores financial statements for (see the Fundamentals entry), and only a symbol with at least one stored transaction is classified: any other symbol reads **Insufficient data**, which is not the same as "no insider trading". Over the last 90 days, by transaction date, it counts the distinct people who bought (transaction code P) and who sold (code S): 3 or more buyers read **1.00 (cluster buy)**; 1 or 2 buyers **0.50 (single buy)**; with no buyers, 3 or more sellers **−1.00 (cluster sell)**; anything else **0.00 (neutral)**. Any purchase outranks sales, so one buyer among ten sellers reads single buy. It counts people, not shares or dollars, and it does not ask why: small regular purchases and pre-planned sales count the same as any other. TSM's rows, for example, are mostly purchases the company's employee stock purchase plan makes on the officers' behalf once a month, about thirty people at one price, on terms the company set in advance; they read as cluster buy.

**News sentiment (7d)** and **News sentiment (30d)** — the average sentiment score of the company's news over the last 7 and 30 days, from Alpha Vantage's per-company scores: **positive** at 0.15 or more, **negative** at −0.15 or less, **neutral** in between. Today both read **Insufficient data** for every symbol, because no scored headlines are stored: the download runs once a day, only for the stocks and funds on Followed Symbols, and it shares the provider's free-plan limit of 25 requests a day with the company-overview download, which runs first and uses the limit up, so the news requests are turned away.

**R&D intensity** — research and development spending as a share of revenue (the sub-line reads "R&D as % of revenue"), both from the company's latest annual report: **high** at 10% or more, **moderate** from 3% up to 10%, **low** below 3%. Normal R&D spending differs widely between industries — a chip designer and an oil producer are not comparable — and the bands do not adjust for that. A company that reports no separate R&D line, or has no reported statements in the app's data, shows "—".

blocks.text: The **Context vs benchmark** card sets the symbol against the market as a whole. Most of it is market-wide and reads the same on every symbol's page; only Price phase and Drawdown from peak are about this symbol. Labels are the stored codes with the underscores shown as spaces — for example late cycle stretched. The two market-wide classifications carry the same status icon as the Daily Market Report: a circled tick for constructive, a circled dash for neutral, a warning triangle for stressed, a dashed circle for no data, taken from the tone the app stored with the label, never re-judged by the page. What each market-wide label means is explained in this Handbook's Daily Market Report section, under Market Cycle (market-wide) and Macro Correlations Regime; the Daily Market Report shows the labels the same way, underscores as spaces.
