items: **Benchmark** — the instrument the market cycle is measured on: SPY, the fund that tracks the S&P 500.

**Market cycle (market-wide)** — the Daily Market Report's Market Cycle composite: SPY's own price phase blended with four macro stances (growth, monetary policy, inflation and global stress) into one of twelve phase codes, such as late cycle stretched. It is the same on every page and says nothing about this symbol.

**Price phase** — this symbol's own position, from its daily closes: **crash** when the close is 12% or more below the highest high of the last 10 sessions, or 10% or more below the close 5 sessions earlier; otherwise, by drawdown from peak, **bear** at −20% or worse, **correction** at −10% or worse, **pullback** at −3% or worse; otherwise **bull extended** (a close at least 5% above its 200-session average), **bull** (at or above that average) or **below 200-day average** (below it). It is worked out only for the instruments the Daily Market Report shows a price phase for — its tracked instruments and your Watchlist symbols — and only when at least 200 daily bars are stored; every other symbol shows "—".

**Drawdown from peak** — how far the latest close sits below the highest high of the last 252 sessions (about a year): −4.63% means 4.63% below that peak. Shown for the same symbols as Price phase, otherwise "—".
**Macro correlations regime** — the Daily Market Report's reading of how the macro picture fits together, for example global liquidity stress, with its status icon. Market-wide.

**Relative strength (20d)** — meant to compare the symbol's move over 20 sessions with the benchmark's, in percentage points (the sub-line reads "vs benchmark, percentage points"). The app does not compute it yet, so it always shows "—".

blocks.text: *What this part of Stock Detail is for:* this is the one section that shows traditional technical-analysis signals — chart patterns, liquidity sweeps, order blocks, and a combined BUY_WATCH / TRIM_WATCH label. It has its own accent colour on purpose: everything above it is a plain reading of stored data; this section is pattern-matching, and it was tested.
What you see here

items: **Flagged readings** — technical readings that currently carry a severity (for example an active Bollinger squeeze, or RSI past its overbought/oversold threshold), repeated here from the technical grid so this section is the one place to see what is currently flagged.

**Chart patterns** — the pattern name, whether it is *confirmed* (for head & shoulders: the neckline has been broken; for triangles: price has broken out) or *unconfirmed*, and a severity badge. Flags have no confirmation step: detection is the signal.

**Action signal** — BUY_WATCH or TRIM_WATCH from the liquidity-sweep rule, with its reasoning lines and a confluence score out of 4 (sweep, close back across the swept level, an order block, the trend). Shown as plain "3/4", not a meter: it is a count of conditions, not a confidence level.

blocks.text: What testing found

Before any result was looked at, eleven hypotheses were written down, one per signal type. Each one tested whether the signal predicts a move of at least 3% in its claimed direction over the next 10 trading sessions. The test used about ten years of daily bars for 2,482 US stocks, and the bar for "meaningful" was fixed in advance.

items: **RSI oversold** (predicting a rise) was the only one to clear the bar on the main data, and only just (1.256 against a floor of 1.25). On the held-out period that had never been looked at, it fell to 1.153. That's below the floor, and statistically indistinguishable from no effect. **Not confirmed.**

**None of the other ten showed a meaningful effect.** RSI overbought was measurable but below the floor. MACD crosses, flags, head & shoulders and liquidity sweeps sat at or near no effect. A Bollinger squeeze was followed by slightly *smaller* moves, not larger ones.

**The BUY_WATCH / TRIM_WATCH labels** did no better than the best single signal. That result is about *this specific rule as built*, which has known weaknesses. It is not a verdict on combining signals in general.

blocks.text: Not tested
Triangles (ascending, descending, symmetrical) and double tops/bottoms appear in this section but were not part of the testing. The same caution applies to them, with no result behind it either way.
How to read this section

Everything here is still shown, exactly as built, because a visible, labelled null result is more useful than a hidden signal. Read it as a description of what the chart looks like, not as a forecast.

sections.title: Watchlist
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* the Watchlist is your list of symbols to keep an eye on, newest first, with the same market columns as Today's Candidates, read the same way. It is saved to one shared list until sign-in exists. Adding a symbol also queues its data: the data workers fetch it within a few minutes and it is then computed, so a newly added symbol fills in on its own. Like the rest of the app it describes stored data and does not recommend anything.

blocks.text: Each row shows the symbol, company and exchange, then **Close**, **Change %**, **RVOL**, **$ Volume**, **Market cap**, **RSI**, **Breakout**, **% of 52w high**, **Catalyst** and **Score**, with the same formulas, formats and tooltips as the candidates list, then **Added** (the day the symbol was added), **Compute** and **Remove**. A close that is not from the latest expected session carries a neutral "as of" date so an old price never reads as current. **Score** is shown only for a symbol that is one of today's candidates; any other row reads "—", never 0.
While a symbol has no stored data at all its row reads "No price data" and all market columns read "—"; this lasts only until its first fetch arrives.

The scanner covers US common stocks only, so a symbol outside its universe — an ADR such as TSMC (TSM) or BP, for example — has no scanner reading. For such a symbol the row is worked out when the page loads from the symbol's own stored daily bars (one bar per session, Tiingo first when it has the symbol, otherwise Yahoo Finance — in practice Yahoo Finance for these symbols), with the same formulas the scanner uses: **Close**, **Change %**, **$ Volume**, **RVOL**, **RSI**, **Breakout** and **% of 52w high**. The row is marked "from daily bars" under the company name; its tooltip reads "Outside the scanner's universe: computed from this symbol's own daily bars (source: Yahoo Finance) with the scanner's formulas. Not a scanner reading — no score." Its date follows the symbol's latest daily bar. These figures are worked out each time the list loads and are never stored with the scanner's readings, so they do not change the scanner's coverage count ("X of Y symbols scanned"). Yahoo Finance prices are adjusted for splits but not for dividends, while the scanner reads Tiingo prices adjusted for both, so **% of 52w high** and **Breakout** for such a row are close to, but not strictly comparable with, a scanner row's.

items: **No score** — such a symbol is never a candidate, so Score reads "—".

**Market cap** comes from the fundamentals provider when it is reported in US dollars. When the provider's figure is in another currency (TSMC's is in New Taiwan dollars) or does not reconcile with the US-dollar price (as for BP), the cell reads "—" with a short note such as "Not in USD (TWD) — not converted"; its tooltip gives the full reason. No converted figure is ever shown.

blocks.text: Pick a match from the search, or type a ticker and press Enter. A match outside the scanner's filters is marked "not scanned — from daily bars": it can be added, and its row is then worked out from its own daily bars as above.

Adding a symbol queues its data fetch straight away, without pressing Compute. The row's Compute column shows the progress — **Waiting for data · queued 5:56 PM (added to watchlist)**, then **Computing analysis** — and the row reloads with its new figures once it reads computed, usually within a few minutes (see The Compute button).

sections.title: Followed Symbols and Computed Symbols
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* these two screens, under Tracking next to the Watchlist, show and change which symbols the data pipeline works on. **Followed Symbols** is the list the pipeline fetches and computes every day. **Computed Symbols** lists every symbol it is computing right now and why, including your own **Compute** requests. The app itself never fetches data when you press a button here: it records the request, the data workers fetch on their own schedule, and the daily computation picks the symbol up.

blocks.text: The table lists every followed symbol, newest first: its name, **type** (equity, ETF or crypto), **listing** (US, foreign or crypto), **source** — "Seeded from .env" for the starting list taken from the app's configuration once, when the list was created, or "Added by you" — and the date it was added. For each of them the pipeline fetches and computes daily bars, technical readings, fundamentals, financial statements for equities, and news where the news source supports the symbol.

Two separate searches add a symbol, and they search different sets. **Search the scanner universe** covers the US common stocks the momentum scanner works from; a match the scanner's eligibility filters leave out is marked "not scanned". **Search all symbols — ETFs, ADRs, OTC and crypto** covers every US-listed symbol in the app's symbol directory plus Binance spot pairs, and shows the provider's type (for example ETP or ADR), the asset type, the venue, and "In scanner universe" when the scanner also covers it. Foreign listings (such as 2222.SR) cannot be found by either search yet.

items: **Follow** adds the symbol; a symbol already followed reads "Following". Some listing types (warrants, units and similar) cannot be computed and are refused with "This listing type (warrants, units, …) can't be computed."
**Compute** on a result or a row asks for the symbol to be fetched and computed now — see the Compute entry.
**Unfollow** stops the daily fetching. Anything already computed is kept. A seeded symbol that is unfollowed leaves the list; following it again lists it as "Added by you".

blocks.text: Every symbol with at least one open reason to be computed, shown as tags: **Followed** (on Followed Symbols), **Watchlist**, **Today's candidate** (in today's scanner list) and **Manual** (you pressed Compute). The first three are automatic and come and go with those lists. Computed history is never deleted when a reason closes.

items: **State** — for a queued fetch (a Compute request, or a symbol just added to the Watchlist), where it stands (see the Compute entry); otherwise **Computed**, or **Scheduled · next daily pass** when the symbol has not been computed yet.
**Last computed** — when the daily computation last ran for the symbol, or "not yet".

**Stop computing** — shown only for a Manual reason. It closes only your request: a symbol with another reason stays computed ("Other reasons keep it computed"); one with none leaves the list, and its computed history is kept.

blocks.text: While a queued fetch — a Compute request or a Watchlist addition — is waiting for data or computing, the screen checks again every 12 seconds and says so above the table; otherwise it does not refresh on its own.

**Compute** appears on each Watchlist row, each Followed Symbols row and each result of both searches. It queues the symbol: the data workers fetch its data, then it is computed, usually within two to five minutes. The button is then replaced by the request's state, in your local time:

items: **Waiting for data · requested 5:45 PM** — queued; the data has not been fetched yet. A symbol just added to the Watchlist is queued the same way without pressing Compute, and reads **Waiting for data · queued 5:56 PM (added to watchlist)**.
**Computing analysis** — the data has arrived and the computation picks it up within about a minute.
**Computed 5:49 PM** — done, with a link to Stock Detail for a stock or fund.

**Data hasn't arrived — requested …, waited … min** — the data was still missing after 30 minutes, so the app stops waiting instead of showing a request as in progress forever. **Check again** looks at the same open request once more; it does not start a new fetch.
**Computation failed** — the computation raised an error; open it to read the stored message.

blocks.text: A symbol already computed automatically (followed, on the Watchlist or a candidate) can still be computed: the request asks for a fresh fetch and computation. Pressing Compute again while your request is open keeps that same request; to ask again, use Stop computing on Computed Symbols first.

sections.title: Alarm History
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* Alarm History, under Tracking, lists the alerts the analyst bot's alert scan actually posted to Discord, newest first, in your local time. It is a record of what was posted, not a live scan and not a forecast. The momentum screener's alerts are not included.

entries.title: What is recorded, and since when

blocks.text: An alert is recorded only once its post has gone out: the symbol, whether it is an equity or crypto, the alert type, its severity, the bot's message and the time it fired. An alert the bot detected but could not post is not recorded (it is tried again on the next scan), and the momentum screener's alerts are not recorded at all.

items: **Liquidity sweep** — the bot's liquidity-sweep rule fired on the symbol's bars.
**Bollinger squeeze** — Bollinger Bands are unusually narrow.
**RSI overbought** / **RSI oversold** — RSI (14) is above 70 / below 30 (the bot's default thresholds).
**Fundamental tier flip** — an equity's fundamental composite tier changed to strong or weak.
**VIX elevated** — the VIX is above the bot's threshold; this one is about the whole market.

blocks.text: Under the caveat, the page says when the **records start**: the earliest recorded alert, in your local date and time. Earlier periods have *no record*, which is not the same as no alerts. A date range before that point shows "No alerts in this period" with a note that nothing is recorded that far back.

entries.title: Grouped view and Show every alert

blocks.text: By default the page shows one row per symbol and alert type in the chosen range: when it last fired, the symbol, the alert type, the latest alert's severity and message, and how many times it was posted with the first and last time, for example "×10 · Sep 25, 11:14 PM – Sep 27, 9:32 PM". A row with repeats opens to its individual alerts, five at a time, with **Load older** for the rest.

**Before and after 27 September 2026, 23:52 Greek time (20:52 UTC).** Alerts recorded before then are re-posts, not separate events: the bot posted a condition, waited out a four-hour cooldown for that symbol and alert type, and posted it again if the condition still held. So ×10 in that period usually means one ongoing condition seen ten times, not ten new signals — a liquidity sweep, for instance, could keep firing for many sessions. From that switch on, each alert marks an **onset**: the condition started on the bar shown as "bar …" after at least 5 sessions without it (RSI crossing above 70 or below 30, a Bollinger Squeeze beginning, a new liquidity sweep on the bar, VIX crossing above 25, or a fundamental tier flip). A condition that stays true is not posted again, and the same onset is recorded at most once. The page shows the switch in its note under "Records start".

**Show every alert** switches to the plain list of every post, newest first: fired time, symbol, alert type, severity and message. Both views load 100 rows at a time, and **Load older** adds the next ones below.

Click a column header to sort: **Last fired** (or **Fired**), **Symbol**, **Alert type**, **Severity** (info, then notice, then warning), **Message** (in the grouped view, **Latest message**: the group's newest message) and, in the grouped view, **Repeats**; click again to reverse. Only a group's open/close control does not sort. The search box above the table finds alerts whose symbol, message, severity or alert type (as shown) contains what you type, in upper or lower case; in the grouped view it groups the matching alerts, and an opened group lists those same alerts, newest first.

Unlike the other tables, sorting and searching here run on the server over every alert in your filters, not only the rows already loaded, so the first page of a sorted list really is the top of the whole list, and **Load more** adds the next rows in that order. A sorted or searched list is fixed at the moment it first loaded: alerts that arrive later are not slipped in between its pages, so no row is skipped or shown twice. The next automatic check (see Links and refreshing) starts it again from its first page, now including them. A search can be up to 60 characters. The default is the grouped view, newest first, with no search.

items: **Symbol** — one symbol, for example AAPL or BTCUSDT, applied as you type.
**Type** — any of the alert types that have ever been recorded; none selected means all.
**Severity** — info, notice or warning; none selected means all.
**Date range** — From and To are whole days in your local time, both included. The default is the last 7 days, today included; **Last 7 days** goes back to it.

blocks.text: Changing a filter starts the list again from its first page and closes any opened groups. The filters, the view (grouped or every alert), the sort and the search are kept in the page's address, so going back to the page — for example with **← Back to Alarm History** on Stock Detail — shows the same list. A filter the app rejects, such as a symbol with characters no symbol has, is explained in plain words in place of the list.

items: **info** — worth knowing, not urgent (a Bollinger squeeze).
**notice** — worth a second look (RSI overbought or oversold, a liquidity sweep, a fundamental tier flip to strong).
**warning** — actively flagged as elevated risk or urgency (VIX elevated, a fundamental tier flip to weak).

blocks.text: Severity is fixed by the alert type (for a tier flip, by its direction). It says how much attention the bot's rule asks for, not how likely anything is to happen. The badge always shows the word next to its colour.
Most of these alerts are classical technical-analysis conditions, so the page opens with the same caveat as Stock Detail's Classical Technical Signals section, word for word:

For a stock or fund, the symbol links to its Stock Detail page, opened at the Classical Technical Signals section. Crypto symbols have no Stock Detail page and are not linked. Neither is a market-wide alert such as VIX elevated: it is about the whole market, even though it is recorded under the symbol whose scan noticed it (the row says "market-wide").

Nothing is pushed to the page. It checks for new alerts when you come back to its tab and every 60 seconds while it is open and visible, and shows **Last checked** with the time of the latest successful check. In the default newest-first list, a check re-reads only the newest rows and adds new ones on top; rows you loaded with Load older and groups you opened stay as they are. In a sorted or searched list, a check starts the list again from its first page, as of that moment. If a check fails, the rows stay and the page says it couldn't check.

sections.title: Tracked Positions
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* Tracked Positions, under Tracking, follows every alert the momentum scanner raised — each symbol that passed all of the scanner's gates on a session — through the pre-registered exit rules, until one of those rules closes it. It is research instrumentation: a record of how the alerts behaved afterwards, kept to judge the exit rules themselves. It is not a portfolio. Nothing was bought or sold, and its percentages are price moves from the alert-day close, not results of any trade.

blocks.text: The daily chain runs once a session's bars have landed: bar ingestion, then the momentum scanner, then the tracker. The tracker first evaluates every active row against the new session, then opens one row for each of that session's gate-pass alerts. A symbol alerted on more than one session therefore has one row per alert, and can appear twice.

The page has two tabs, **Active** (the default) and **Closed**, each with its count, for example "Active (20)" and "Closed (16)". Both lists show the most recent alert first. Nothing is pushed to the page: it re-reads the list when you come back to its browser tab, and if that fails the rows stay and the page says it couldn't check.

items: **Symbol / Exchange / Bucket** — the ticker, company, exchange, and the scanner bucket it was alerted in (Market or Penny). The ticker opens the symbol's Stock Detail page.
**Alerted Date** — the session the alert was raised on.
**Closed Date** (Closed) — the session the exit rule fired on, the one Exit % is measured at.

**Sessions Elapsed** — how many trading sessions the exit rules have evaluated since the alert. Trading sessions follow the NYSE calendar, so weekends and market holidays never count. On a closed row it is the count at which it closed.
**Reference Price** — the close on the alert date, as traded. Every percentage on the page is measured from it.
**Current Price** (Active) — the close on the latest scan date.
**Unrealized %** (Active) — the current price against the reference price: (current ÷ reference − 1) × 100.
**Exit Reason** (Closed) — the exit rule that closed the row, as its plain name, for example breakout_failed.
**Exit %** (Closed) — the close on the session the rule fired against the reference price, measured the same way.

blocks.text: Only **Unrealized %** and **Exit %** are coloured, green up and red down, like Change % on the candidates list: they are price facts, not signals. Everything else, including the exit reason, is neutral text with no badge or icon.

A row opened on the latest session has not been through the exit rules yet: the tracker first evaluates a row on the session after its alert. Its **Sessions Elapsed** reads "Not yet evaluated" and its **Unrealized %** reads "—", never 0 or 0.0%, because there is no reading yet; its Current Price is the alert-day close itself. One note above the Active table counts these rows, for example "10 rows have not been evaluated yet — the next tracker run evaluates them."

Separately, a single active row can lag the others — for example when its symbol has no bar for the latest session. The tracker then has not evaluated that row through the latest scan, and its Sessions Elapsed carries a neutral note, "as of" the last session it was evaluated on, so a lagging count never reads as current.
Each session the tracker checks an active row against the exit rules in this order, and the first one that matches closes it:

items: **breakout_failed** — the close fell back below the 20-day resistance level the symbol broke out over at the alert. Measured to fire on the first session in most cases (651 of 1,545 replayed exits, at a median peak of 0.00%), so it is an overly sensitive rule, not a confirmed breakout failure.
**lost_vwap** — the close fell below its rolling 20-day VWAP (volume-weighted average price). A plain definition; no finding qualifies it.
**momentum_stalled** — relative volume (20-day) stayed below 1.5 for 3 sessions in a row. A plain definition; no finding qualifies it.

**stop_atr** — the close fell more than 2 × ATR(14) below the reference price. In the replay this condition was true 116 times but fired first only 31 times: faster rules usually close the row before it, and the order of the rules is itself unvalidated.
**timeout** — 20 sessions passed without another exit firing. It never fired in 1,545 replayed exits (the longest ran 17 sessions), so a timeout here is itself unusual.

blocks.text: Click a row's Exit Reason (or press Enter or Space on it) to open that rule's note in a panel directly under the row; it stays open until you click it again. Each note is specific to its rule — there is no single blanket warning — and the lost_vwap and momentum_stalled notes are just their definitions.

entries.title: When the daily chain is behind

blocks.text: If the daily chain itself has stalled — for example because the bars did not arrive — every row is old at once. The page then shows one note above the tabs, in neutral styling (no data is wrong, it is old):

items: **No new scan** — "No new scan for 2 trading sessions — the latest is Sep 25, 2026. Tracked figures below are as of that date." Shown when at least one expected session has no scan yet; it says "1 trading session" for one. If the machine was asleep over the close, the session is caught up automatically once its bars land (for sessions in the last five), and the note clears then; the Data Source page marks that session "Caught up late (not clean)".

**Tracking behind** — "The Sep 28, 2026 scan exists but tracking has not been updated since Sep 25, 2026." Shown when the latest scan finished more than 15 minutes ago without the tracker completing for it, or the chain deferred that session because its bars had not landed in time.

blocks.text: If both apply, only "No new scan" is shown. Both count trading sessions on the NYSE calendar, so a weekend or holiday never raises them, and both come from the chain's own records, never from the rows' dates. The per-row notes stay as they are while the banner shows.

sections.title: Data Source
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* the Data Source page shows whether the app's data is arriving: how much of each provider's daily budget is used, and how the daily chain — bar ingestion, then the momentum scanner, then the tracker — ran for each recent NYSE session.

blocks.text: Each row of the daily chain table is one closed NYSE session, newest first. Its **Status** is one of seven, in plain text with no colour:

items: **Clean** — the scanner and the tracker both finished for the session on the first attempt, with no error.
**Recovered (after N attempts)** — both finished, but only after one or more retries; the last error before recovery is shown beneath the row.

**Caught up late (not clean)** — both finished, but late: the session's window had passed (for example, the machine was asleep over the close), so momentum-daily ran it by catch-up once its bars had landed. The scan still uses only data up to that session. It never counts as a clean session, and the Discord bot does not post alerts from a catch-up scan. Beneath the row, **Deferred** says why it was put off (for example, the bars had not reached 95% coverage in time); if no reason was recorded, the last error before the catch-up is shown instead. **Attempts** counts the in-window and catch-up attempts together.
**In progress** — the session's window is still open and the chain has not finished it yet.
**Failed** — the chain gave up on the session, or started it and never finished; the reason is shown beneath the row.
**Not run — no attempt was recorded** — nothing ran for the session: momentum-daily was not running, or the machine was off.
**Not recorded (before tracking began)** — the session is older than the chain's own run records, so there is nothing to show.

blocks.text: **Coverage now** is computed when the page asks, so it can differ from the coverage the run saw at the time.

sections.title: Using the tables
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* every table in the app — Today's Candidates, Watchlist, Followed Symbols, Computed Symbols, Alarm History, Tracked Positions and the Data Source daily chain — sorts, searches and links the same way. Sorting only reorders rows; it never ranks them by how good they are.

blocks.text: Click a column header to sort by it; click it again to reverse. The sorted column shows ▲ or ▼, the others a faint two-way mark. Every column sorts except action columns (Remove, Unfollow, Stop computing) and, in Alarm History, a group's open/close control. A value shown as "—" (or "not yet", "not computed", "Not yet evaluated") always goes to the bottom, whichever way you sort, and rows with the same value are ordered by symbol (in the daily chain, newest session first).

items: **Today's Candidates** — by RVOL, highest first; the score keeps its "unvalidated" label in every order.
**Watchlist** and **Followed Symbols** — the newest added first.
**Computed Symbols** — the most recently computed first; "not yet" last.
**Alarm History** — newest first (the grouped view by when a group last fired).
**Tracked Positions** — the most recent alert first, on both tabs.
**Data Source daily chain** — the newest session first.

**Compute** and **State** columns sort by computation state: what needs attention first (failed, data hasn't arrived), then what is waiting or computing, then scheduled and computed. The daily chain's **Status** sorts the same way: not run and failed first, then in progress, recovered, caught up late and clean, and not recorded last.

blocks.text: Two lists keep a fixed order and do not sort: the Backtest Lab's hypotheses (the order they were registered in) and Stock Detail's score breakdown (the model's own order).

The search box above a table keeps the rows where any column's text, as shown on screen, contains what you type — a symbol, a company name, a date such as "Sep 24", a label such as "Crypto" or "Recovered" — in upper or lower case. While it filters it says how many rows match, for example "3 of 20 rows"; Esc or the × clears it. It searches the rows the page has loaded. Alarm History is the exception: its search and its sorting run on the server over every alert in your filters, and a sorted or searched list stays as it was when it first loaded until the next check (see Sorting and searching alerts under Alarm History).

A symbol that is a stock or a fund links to its Stock Detail page. Crypto pairs (such as BTCUSDT), Treasury yields and market-wide rows (the VIX, VIX elevated alerts) have no Stock Detail page, so they are plain text. Each table's sort and search — and, on a page with tabs, the open tab — are kept in the page's address, and Stock Detail offers **← Back to …** naming the page you came from (Watchlist, Followed Symbols, Computed Symbols, Alarm History, Tracked Positions, Daily Market Report or Candidates). It returns you to the same view, sorted and searched as you left it.

sections.title: Claude connector
sections.intro: *What this is for:* the platform can be read from claude.ai through a custom connector (an MCP server, svc-mcp). Claude sees the same data as the app's pages, read-only, after you sign in with your GitHub account.

entries.title: What Claude can see through the connector

blocks.text: The connector gives Claude ten read-only tools. Each one returns the same data as a page of this app, at the moment Claude asks:

items: **Daily market report**: the Daily Market Report page.
**Alerts**: the Alarm History page, as individual alerts or grouped by symbol and alert type, with the same filters (symbol, alert type, severity, date range).
**Today's candidates** and **one candidate**: the Today's Candidates page and a candidate's row.

**Symbol analysis**: the Stock Detail analysis, including the chart patterns, the BUY/TRIM action signal and the latest cash-flow statement. If the analysis is stale it is computed on demand, as when you open the page; Claude may be told it is still computing.
**Watchlist**: the Watchlist page. Claude can read it but cannot add or remove symbols.
**Tracked positions**: the Tracked Positions page (active, closed or all).
**Data-source status**: the Data Source page, including each session's chain status.
**Handbook**: the list of Handbook sections, and any one section or entry by id, so Claude can explain a screen in this Handbook's own words.

blocks.text: Nothing Claude does through the connector can change the platform: every tool only reads, and the server that answers Claude cannot reach the app's add, remove or follow actions. Replies never include keys or passwords; anything that looks like one is removed before it leaves the server.
Claude is given the same claims the app makes, word for word, before it sees any data:
Only your GitHub account can connect. The server records each request's time, source address and which tool was called, never what it returned.
